title: Chapter XXVI
paragraphs: Summer was already past its height when Edgar reluctantly gave in to their pleas, and Catherine and I set out on our first ride to meet her cousin. The day was close and sultry, without sunshine, though the sky was too hazy and mottled to promise rain. We had agreed to meet at the guidepost by the crossroads. But when we arrived, a little herd-boy sent to meet us said, “Master Linton's just this side o' t' Heights, and he'd be much obliged if ye'd come a bit further.”
“Then Master Linton has forgotten his uncle's very first instruction,” I said. “He told us to stay on Grange land, and we're leaving it already.”
“Well, once we reach him we'll turn the horses towards home,” my companion answered. “That's the direction we'll take for our ride.”

But when we found him, scarcely a quarter of a mile from his own door, he had no horse. We had to dismount and let ours graze. He was lying on the heather waiting for us, and did not get up until we were only a few yards away. His steps were so weak and his face so pale that I exclaimed at once, “Why, Master Heathcliff, you're in no state to enjoy a walk this morning. How ill you look!”

Catherine looked at him in sorrow and astonishment. The joyful greeting on her lips became a cry of alarm, and instead of celebrating their long-delayed meeting she anxiously asked whether he was worse than usual.

“No—better—better!” he gasped, trembling and holding on to her hand as though he needed it to support him. His large blue eyes moved timidly over her. The hollows around them had changed their once languid expression into something haggard and wild.
“But you have been worse,” his cousin insisted. “Worse than when I last saw you. You're thinner, and—”
“I'm tired,” he interrupted quickly. “It's too hot to walk. Let's rest here. And I often feel sick in the mornings. Papa says it's because I'm growing so fast.”
Far from reassured, Cathy sat down, and he lay beside her.

“This is rather like your paradise,” she said, trying to sound cheerful. “Do you remember the two days we agreed to spend in the places and ways each of us liked best? This is almost your day, except for the clouds. But they're so soft and gentle that it's nicer than sunshine. Next week, if you're able, we'll ride down to the Grange park and try mine.”

Linton did not seem to remember what she meant, and clearly found any sort of conversation a great effort. His indifference to the subjects she raised, and his complete inability to offer anything to entertain her, were so obvious that she could not hide her disappointment. Some indefinable change had come over his whole appearance and manner. The petulance that affection could turn to tenderness had given way to listless apathy. He seemed less like an irritable child who frets and teases to be comforted, and more like a chronic invalid, sullenly absorbed in himself, rejecting comfort and ready to take anyone else's cheerful laughter as an insult. Catherine saw as clearly as I did that he found our company more of a punishment than a pleasure, and before long she freely suggested leaving. Unexpectedly, the suggestion roused him from his lethargy and made him strangely agitated. He glanced towards the Heights in fear and begged her to stay at least another half-hour.

“But I think you'd be more comfortable at home than sitting here,” Cathy said. “I can see my stories and songs and chatter aren't amusing you today. You've grown wiser than I have in these six months; you don't much care for my amusements now. If I could entertain you, I'd gladly stay.”

“Stay and rest yourself,” he replied. “And, Catherine, don't think or say I'm _very_ ill. It's the muggy weather and the heat that make me so dull. And before you came I walked about quite a lot—for me. Tell uncle I'm fairly well, will you?”
“I'll tell him _you_ say so, Linton. I couldn't tell him you are,” my young mistress said, puzzled that he kept insisting on something so plainly untrue.

“And come back here next Thursday,” he went on, avoiding her bewildered eyes. “Thank him for letting you come—thank him very much, Catherine. And—and if you _did_ happen to meet my father and he asked about me, don't let him think I've been terribly quiet and stupid. Don't look sad and downhearted the way you _are_ looking. He'll be angry.”
“I don't care if he's angry,” Cathy cried, thinking his anger would be directed at her.
“But I do,” her cousin said with a shudder. “_Don't_ turn him against me, Catherine. He's very harsh.”
“Does he treat you harshly, Master Heathcliff?” I asked. “Has he tired of indulging you and begun to act on his hatred, instead of merely feeling it?”

Linton looked at me without answering. Cathy stayed beside him another ten minutes. His head drooped sleepily onto his chest, and he made no sound except muffled groans of exhaustion or pain. Then she tried to find some consolation in gathering bilberries and sharing her finds with me. She offered him none, seeing that any further attention would only tire and annoy him.
“Has it been half an hour yet, Ellen?” she whispered in my ear at last. “I don't know why we're staying. He's asleep, and papa will want us home.”
“Well, we can't leave him sleeping,” I answered. “Be patient and wait until he wakes. You were so eager to set out, but your longing to see poor Linton has worn off quickly enough!”

“Why did _he_ want to see me?” Catherine replied. “I liked him better in his worst tempers before than I do in this strange mood. It's as though seeing us were a task he's being forced to do for fear his father will scold him. But I'm certainly not coming here to please Mr. Heathcliff, whatever reason he has for making Linton go through this punishment. And although I'm glad his health is better, I'm sorry he's so much less pleasant and so much less affectionate towards me.”
“So you think his health _has_ improved?” I said.
“Yes,” she answered. “You know how he always made so much of his suffering. He's not fairly well, as he wanted me to tell papa, but he's probably better.”
“I don't agree with you there, Miss Cathy,” I said. “I should think he's much worse.”
At that moment Linton woke with a start, bewildered and terrified, and asked whether someone had called his name.
“No,” Catherine said, “unless it was in your dreams. I don't understand how you can fall asleep outdoors in the morning.”
“I thought I heard my father,” he gasped, looking up at the dark, overhanging crag above us. “Are you sure no one spoke?”

“Quite sure,” his cousin replied. “Ellen and I were only disagreeing about your health. Are you really stronger than when we last met in winter, Linton? If you are, there's one thing I'm certain hasn't grown stronger: your affection for me. Tell me—are you?”
Tears streamed from Linton's eyes as he answered, “Yes, yes, I am!” Still gripped by the voice he had imagined, he kept looking up and down for the person it belonged to.

Cathy stood up. “We must say goodbye for today,” she said. “I won't pretend I haven't been terribly disappointed by our meeting, though I won't tell anyone but you. That's not because I'm afraid of Mr. Heathcliff.”

“Hush!” Linton murmured. “For God's sake, hush! He's coming.” He clung to Catherine's arm, trying to hold her back, but at those words she quickly pulled free and whistled to Minny, who came to her like a dog.
“I'll be here next Thursday,” she called, springing into the saddle. “Goodbye. Hurry, Ellen!”
And so we left him. He was hardly aware that we were going, so completely was he occupied by the thought of his father's approach.

Before we reached home, Catherine's annoyance had softened into a confused mixture of pity and regret, mingled with vague, uneasy doubts about Linton's real condition, both in his health and his life at home. I shared those doubts, but advised her to say little: another visit would help us judge better. My master asked how our outing had gone. We duly passed on his nephew's thanks, and Miss Cathy touched lightly on the rest. My answers gave him little more information, for I hardly knew what I should conceal and what I should reveal.
